blocks.text: Now, if the matter is decided by authority, the Vulgate agrees with both Arabic versions, in which معرون [maʿrūn] is the cerastes, like Avicenna's مقرنة [muqarrana]. In those languages Koph and Ajin are not rarely interchanged. Hence among the Chaldeans and Syrians earth is called ܐܪܥܐ [III, 207] and ܐܬܢܢ; to smoke, ܩܘܦܣ and ܟܦܣ; cold, ܩܘܦܣܐ and ܟܦܣܐ. And in Jonathan רקם is the same place that the Hebrews call עצמון, Num. XXXIV, 4. In the same way among the Arabs horn is both عرن [ʿarn] and قرن [qarn]. Giggeius, from Alcamus: عران البقر [ʿirān al-baqar] [col. 418] the horns of oxen, عرنة [ʿirna] the root of the horns, عرون [ʿarūn] the slug, the snail, namely ^{c)} because of the two little horns with which it feels its way, since it lacks the use of eyes. By the same reasoning the cerastes is called both مقرن [muqarran] and معرون [maʿrūn], that is, horned, or having little horns like those of a snail ^{(1)}. Aelian: Ὑπὲρ τοῦ μετώπου κέρατα ἔχει δύο, καὶ ἔοικε τοῖς κοχλίου τὰ κέρατα, οὐ μέν ἐστι ὡς ἐκεῖνα ἁπαλά· [Hyper tou metōpou kerata echei dyo, kai eoike tois kochliou ta kerata, ou men esti hōs ekeina hapala] Above its forehead it has two horns, similar to the horns of a snail, though not equally soft. Pliny, however, in book 11, chapter 37, says that the horns of both the cerastes and the snail are corporeal, that is, fleshy. Accordingly Belon does not call them horns, but small protuberances like grains of barley, which resemble little horns ^{(2)}. Hence it is evident that those ^{d)} are not a little mistaken who write that knife handles for the tables of emperors are made from the horns of cerastes, because they betray poison placed nearby by sweating. For who would make knife handles out of so tiny a horn, and a soft one at that? Not to mention that it is not reasonable that the little horns of a poisonous animal should have an ἀλεξιφάρμακος [alexipharmakos] power. But the barbarous writers wrongly attribute to the horns of the cerastes what they had read somewhere about the horn of the كركدان [karkadān] carcaddan, or monoceros. Of it, namely, the Nubian Geographer, Clim. 1, section 8: ملوك الهند [III, 208] تصنع من قرن هذه الذابة انصبة السكاكين للموايد فانا وضع الطعام بين ايديهم وكان فيه سم عرق ذلك النصاب فيعلم بذلك ان الطعام مسموم [mulūk al-hind taṣnaʿ min qarn hādhihi al-dhāba anṣibat al-sakākīn lil-mawāyid fa-anā wuḍiʿa al-ṭaʿām bayna aydīhim wa-kāna fīhi samm ʿariqa dhālika al-niṣāb fa-yuʿlam bi-dhālika anna al-ṭaʿām masmūm] The kings of India have knife handles made for themselves from the horn of this animal for use at table. And when food is set before them, if it is poisoned, those handles become moist with sweat. From this it is detected that the food is infected with poison. Did Epiphanius have something of this kind in mind when, writing against the Pneumatomachi, he mentions κεράστου δεινοῦ μονοκέρωτος [kerastou deinou monokerōtos], of the dread one-horned cerastes? I do not think so; rather, in his opinion the serpent cerastes is one-horned. For he says the same about the heresy of the Basilidians: Ὡς κεράστου τρόπον ἐν ἄμμῳ κεχωσμένη, διὰ δὲ τοῦ κέρατος ἐν ἀέρι προκύπτουσα, καὶ τὸν ὄλεθρον τοῖς περιτυγχάνουσιν αὐτὴν ἐργαζομένη· [Hōs kerastou tropon en ammō kechōsmenē, dia de tou keratos en aeri prokyptousa, kai ton olethron tois peritynchanousin autēn ergazomenē] Buried in the sand like the cerastes, with its horn thrust up into the air, deadly to those who come upon it.

To return to the matter: it has so far remained uncertain whether the sephiphon is the cerastes or the haemorrhous, since much favors each interpretation. We have said that Jerome and both Arabic versions render it cerastes, and that this interpretation agrees excellently with the words of the Patriarch. Yet the sipphon, a similar word, is so described by the Arabs that it seems rather to be the haemorrhous. What if we say that sephiphon is a name common to both? That certainly seems to be so. And hardly anyone will call this into doubt who knows how similar the cerastes and the haemorrhous are. Each is a species of viper. Both are sand-colored, but the haemorrhous is spotted. Both are of the same size. Avicenna on the haemorrhous and the haemorrhois: واطوالها اطوال المقرنه [wa-aṭwāluhā aṭwāl al-muqarrana] Their length is the same as that of the cerastes. Nor does the haemorrhous lack horns, as Aelian testifies in book 15, chapter 13: Φρίττει δὲ τὴν κεφαλὴν οἱονεὶ κέρασί τισιν· [Phrittei de tēn kephalēn hoionei kerasi tisin] Its head bristles as if with certain horns. And long before, Nicander:
Τοῦ μὲν ὑπὲρ νιφόεντα κεράατα δοιὰ μετώπῳ [col. 419] Ἔγκειται· — — — — [Tou men hyper niphoenta keraata doia metōpō enkeitai] Above its forehead two horns are seen, whiter than snow. — — — — —

Thus the haemorrhous is a species of cerastes, or horned serpent. This is especially notable: whereas the other serpents creep straight forward, the cerastes and the haemorrhous alone move with an uncertain and wavering gait, staggering to either side, drunk, so to speak, or like one who limps. Hence Aëtius on the cerastes: It creeps obliquely, not straight. And Isidore: It is more sinuous than other serpents. And Aelian on the haemorrhous too: Λοξὸν δὲ οἶμον πρόεισιν [Loxon de oimon proeisin], It advances by an oblique path. And Nicander, comparing it with the cerastes in this very respect: [III, 209] Δοχμὰ δ᾽ ἐπισκάζει ὀλίγον δέμας, οἷα κεράστης· [Dochma d’ episkazei oligon demas, hoia kerastēs] It limps, bending its short body sideways, like the cerastes.

The cause lies in the vertebrae of the back, which are not bony, as in the rest, but cartilaginous, and so flexible in either direction that there can be no steadiness in their movement. To this point are these words of Lucan:
— — and the cerastes, wandering with twisting spine.
